📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 1941, General Motors hit the open road with its fleet of Futureliners on the Parade of Progress, a movement meant to spread cutting-edge science and technology across America. With their bubble-top cockpits, exhibition-style innards, and shining chrome panels, the Futureliners became as much of a spectacle as the displays on automotive technology, urban engineering, farming, and leisure pursuits carried within. Now, 85 years later, a resurrected Futureliner is carrying the Parade of Progress torch into the 21st Century—starting in Fresh York City.

It has been revealed that like many modern automotive stories, this Futureliner's resurrection began on Facebook Marketplace. When Matt Katz, owner of the Caretakers Collection, was sent a link to an available Futureliner on the online classified site, he jumped into action. Katz was on the phone with the seller in a matter of minutes, and quickly deputized friend and New Jersey car builder Rob Ida to travel up to Massachusetts the following day.

“[The seller] was totally caught off guard that I just called him. He's like, ‘Listen, like it's Monday night. I'm out at an event. You know, call me tomorrow.’ I'm like, ‘No, no, no, I want to make this deal now.’ I just wanted to lock it up,” Katz mentioned to Road & Track. He said he informed the seller that he wanted Ida, with whom Katz had done prior restoration projects, to come check out the Futureliner. “I was like, ‘Let me call [Ida] and get him to come out and inspect it within forty-eight hours. And if all is good, I'll wire you the balance. And if all is not, return the money to me, the deposit, and we'll call it even.’”.

Ida reported back that the Futureliner example was ripe for restoration, but the journey couldn’t begin immediately. First, Ida had to cut a larger opening in his garage to fit the Futureliner through. Standing 11-feet-7-inches tall and 33 feet long, the GM Futureliner is taller than your average school bus, and about as long as an average fire truck. But once the Futureliner had been transported and maneuvered into Ida’s garage, the real work began.

According to recent reports, as it had been owned and restored by the Peter Pan Bus Tech giant in the 1990s, this Futureliner build started out in better shape than most. It had been updated with GM’s post-World War II styling from 1953—a flatter and less regal version of the shape introduced in 1939. Ida and Katz wanted to bring this Futureliner back to its original Harley Earl-designed glory, but there wasn’t an official blueprint to guide them. Ida even reached out to the General Motors Heritage Center, but it had limited information available about the first-generation Futureliner design. So, Ida had to fabricate many of the parts himself. Some era-specific parts even required the creation of bespoke molds, as no replacements were available.

Sources indicate that “We work off imagery, and we work off of any kind of text or information that we can find. Unfortunately, the Thirty-Nine version is much more difficult to find than the Fifty-Three version. Anytime you do a quick search, you're going to find all the white roof Fifty-Three generation-two post-war Futureliner. So that was really the difficult part: digging deep enough to find the Thirty-Nine version,” Ida stated to Road & Track.

“Somewhere in a conversation with Rob, it came to be that we both agreed: let's go back to the bubble. Let's bring it back to Thirty-Nine, and we didn't realize and truly fully appreciate what that meant. Getting the bubble done was just difficult, but we knew what to do, and Rob had experience,” Katz mentioned. “We didn't realize that after we made that decision, everything else would change on the bus. Not just the paint colors, but also the cladding on the side. So, Fifty-Three has seven clads; ours is four. The GM logo on the front. Rob randomly found this old video by a production company called Rose that I discovered, and he poured through it and discovered in a small clip that the GM logo was backlit.”.

In a recent development, once the restoration was complete, Katz and Ida were eager to show off the piece of moving history, and the inaugural Retromobile event in Newly introduced York City was the perfect venue. But the newly revived Futureliner had to make it from Old Bridge, New Jersey, to Manhattan’s Jacob K. Javits Convention Center. There is no shortage of driving obstacles between those two points on a good day in a regular car, so piloting the massive machine was sure to be a challenge—but with Ida and Katz at the helm, however, the journey went smoother than expected. Thanks to dually-style front wheels, power steering, 360-degree cameras, and working air conditioning, driving the Futureliner was an exercise in patience more than anything else.

“So I drove from Columbus Circle to Times Square to Javits. And as a New Yorker, driving it in New York and just seeing people's reactions ... you know, part of the enjoyment is how people react to it. I've never had a reaction like when I was driving it. And then the fact that they closed Times Square for me while we were driving, and for Rob and me ... I couldn't even have fathomed that as a dream,” Katz said.

Recent findings suggest that and the Futureliner’s adventures are far from over. Katz and Ida are currently scheming a cross-country road trip, starting on the East Coast in 2027 and heading west toward GM’s Heritage Center in Sterling, Michigan. After that, the Futureliner will head to California for the 2027 Pebble Beach Concours d’Elegance, with stops at dealerships and historical markers along the way. The Futureliner will then spend some time at the Petersen Automotive Museum in Los Angeles and stick around for the 2028 Summer Olympics before heading back to GM’s Heritage Center. This cross-country journey will be focused on charity efforts for organizations like the Sloan Kettering Institute for Cancer Research, which the original Parade of Progress highlighted. Trust us: if the Futureliner comes to your town, it’s worth seeing in person.

A New York transplant hailing from the Pacific Northwest, Emmet White has a passion for anything that goes: cars, bicycles, planes, and motorcycles. After learning to ride at 17, Emmet worked in the motorcycle industry before joining Autoweek in 2022 and Road & Track in 2024. The woes of alternate side parking have kept his fleet moderate, with a 2014 Volkswagen Jetta GLI and a BMW 318i E30 street parked in his Queens community.

Scientists discover that leukemia can begin developing 50 years before diagnosis

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1574 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A deadly form of blood cancer may begin taking shape more than 50 years before a person is diagnosed, according to fresh research revealing the surprisingly long and predictable path to leukemia.
  • According to recent reports, scientists have reconstructed how acute myeloid leukemia (AML) develops over a lifetime, discovering that in two-thirds of the cases studied, the first genetic mutation that helped drive the cancer appeared before age 20.
  • The findings suggest that doctors may one day be able to identify people at risk of developing leukemia years or even decades before symptoms appear.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A deadly form of blood cancer may begin taking shape more than 50 years before a person is diagnosed, according to fresh research revealing the surprisingly long and predictable path to leukemia.

According to recent reports, scientists have reconstructed how acute myeloid leukemia (AML) develops over a lifetime, discovering that in two-thirds of the cases studied, the first genetic mutation that helped drive the cancer appeared before age 20. These early changes could remain largely unnoticed for decades before eventually contributing to the disease.

The findings suggest that doctors may one day be able to identify people at risk of developing leukemia years or even decades before symptoms appear. They also raise the possibility of preventing the cancer by slowing the growth of abnormal blood cells long before the disease takes hold.

Blood Samples Reveal Leukemia's Hidden History.

Published in Nature, the study was conducted by researchers at the University of Cambridge and University College London (UCL). By examining blood samples collected over many years, including some obtained as long as 15 years before diagnosis, the team pieced together a detailed history of how leukemia develops.

Industry observers note that the scientists treated these stored samples as a kind of genetic fossil record. Using highly sensitive DNA sequencing and mathematical models, they worked backward to estimate when cancer-related mutations first appeared, how rapidly the affected cells multiplied, and how they competed with other blood cells as the disease approached.

AML is an aggressive blood cancer that affects approximately 2,700 people in the UK annually. Its outlook is often poor, with only about one in six patients surviving at least five years after diagnosis.

In a recent development, scientists have long known that many otherwise healthy older adults carry blood cells with mutations associated with leukemia. This condition, called clonal hematopoiesis, does not necessarily lead to cancer. In fact, most people with these mutations never develop AML. Until now, researchers have struggled to understand why some individuals progress to leukemia while others do not, partly because they lacked a detailed record of the genetic changes occurring in the years before diagnosis.

To investigate, the team turned to samples from the UK Collaborative Trial of Ovarian Cancer Screening (UKCTOCS). That project involved approximately 50,000 women who provided blood samples annually for as long as 11 years.

For the newly introduced analysis, researchers examined samples from 47 women who eventually developed AML, with an average age at diagnosis of 72. They compared these findings with samples from 46 similar women who remained free of blood cancer.

Cancer Mutations Can Remain Hidden for Decades.

According to recent reports, the results revealed an extraordinary timeline. In two-thirds of the women who developed AML, the earliest mutation contributing to the disease was estimated to have occurred before their 20th birthday.

At first, the altered blood cells multiplied extremely slowly, sometimes taking several years just to double in number. But as additional cancer-driving mutations accumulated, their growth accelerated dramatically.

Each newly introduced mutation typically increased the rate of growth by roughly two to three times. By the time cells had acquired four mutations capable of driving cancer, their populations could double within weeks instead of years.

Perhaps even more surprising was how consistently these populations behaved.

Researchers found that groups of genetically related blood cells, known as clones, generally expanded at predictable rates once they became established. Their growth tended to slow only when they faced limited space or competition from another clone that was multiplying more quickly.

Sources indicate that this consistency could have key medical implications. By measuring the growth of a particular clone using just a few blood samples, scientists may be able to estimate how large that population will become many years into the future, potentially even decades later.

A Hidden Warning Sign of Leukemia.

The researchers also identified a striking pattern that appeared in some patients well before leukemia was diagnosed.

In at least one-third of AML cases, a single population of mutated blood cells had grown so extensively that it dominated the blood years before diagnosis. Scientists call this process a "somatic sweep.".

None of the women in the comparison group who remained free of blood cancer indicated the same pattern.

The researchers then examined data from the UK Biobank and confirmed that people showing evidence of these sweeps faced a substantially greater risk of developing AML.

Sources indicate that this finding suggests that somatic sweeps could serve as an important early warning sign. However, conventional genetic testing can miss them because the mutations involved are sometimes incorrectly classified as inherited genetic variations.

Professor Jamie Blundell, who led the research at the University of Cambridge's Early Cancer Institute, explained how the team reconstructed the disease's history.

"Serial blood samples are a fossil record of the blood's evolution. They let us go back in time and reconstruct when each mutation arose and how fast it grew. What surprised us most is how predictable the growth of these clones is. Once a clone is established, its growth rate today tells you where it will be years, even decades, from now.".

In a recent development, he added: "Because the growth is exponential, even modestly slowing a high-risk clone over the decade or more before diagnosis could substantially reduce the chance it becomes leukemia. This opens up strategies we can exploit to prevent these clones ever becoming leukemia.".

Could Leukemia Be Prevented Before It Develops?

The discovery could change how doctors approach a disease that often appears to develop with little warning.

Industry observers note that dr. Caroline Watson, the study's first author and a researcher at the Early Cancer Institute, emphasized the contrast between the sudden impact of a leukemia diagnosis and the decades of biological changes that may precede it.

"As a hematologist, I've seen how suddenly AML can change someone's life. This study reveals that the changes leading to AML can build over decades, with the affected cells growing in surprisingly predictable ways.".

Recent findings suggest that watson is also an Honorary Consultant Haematologist who treats patients at the Cambridge Clonal Haematopoiesis Clinic at Addenbrooke's Hospital. The clinic is the first in Europe dedicated to leukemia prevention and already monitors people whose blood cell mutations place them at increased risk of developing the disease.

She added: "At our clinic, we already assess and monitor people who carry blood-cell mutations that increase their risk of leukemia. Today's findings give us real hope of improving how we identify which of them are at greatest risk and point to a window in which prevention could one day be possible.".

Years of Blood Samples Unlock Newly introduced Cancer Clues.

A major reason the researchers could reconstruct leukemia's development was the availability of blood samples collected repeatedly from the same individuals over many years.

Professor Usha Menon of the UCL Institute of Clinical Trials and Methodology, who led the original UKCTOCS project, highlighted the unexpected scientific value of those samples.

"While UKCTOCS was designed to assess ovarian cancer screening, a key outcome was the establishment of a unique bioresource of serial serum samples. This resource has provided unprecedented opportunities to study how cancers develop over time and to discover and validate biomarkers for earlier detection. We owe an enormous debt of gratitude to the participants whose willingness to contribute their samples and data over many years made this possible. Their generosity is the foundation of this achievement.".

According to recent reports, the women who developed AML received their diagnoses between ages 53 and 83. Because the researchers did not have blood samples taken at the time of diagnosis, they could not directly examine the final stage of the disease's development in those patients.

Sources indicate that the findings also indicated that not every case followed the same extended timeline of detectable changes. In approximately one in five cases, growing populations of mutated blood cells became detectable only one to two years before diagnosis. This suggests that some patients may have a much shorter opportunity for early intervention.

A Newly introduced Path Toward Preventing Leukemia.

Despite these limitations, the results offer an encouraging possibility: leukemia risk might be reduced by intervening long before the disease develops.

Sources indicate that according to the researchers' mathematical models, even a modest reduction in the growth of high-risk blood cell clones could have a substantial effect over time. Because these cells multiply exponentially, slowing their expansion across the ten or more years between a second cancer-driving mutation and diagnosis could significantly reduce the likelihood that they eventually progress to leukemia.

This raises the prospect of preventive treatments designed to restrain dangerous cell populations rather than waiting until they have developed into cancer.

The next challenge is determining whether such an approach can be used safely and effectively in people identified as having an elevated risk of AML. Although the research provides a promising framework for earlier detection and prevention, clinical studies will be needed to establish whether slowing these abnormal cells actually prevents leukemia in humans.

The research was primarily supported by UK Research & Innovation and Cancer Research UK.

Materials provided by University of Cambridge. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Patch 1.3.5.0 for Escape From Tarkov marks the end of its traditional Halloween event, which means Scav violence is back to its normal levels.
  • The highlight of the update is on the performance side, where Battlestate Games has unlocked improved frames across the board, thanks in part to an engine upgrade that finally brings Escape From Tarkov to current-gen standards.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that halloween has ended, making way for jollier celebrations and bigger gifts. In the communal spirit of Thanksgiving week, which is absolutely not a thing in Russia, Escape from Tarkov has dropped one of its biggest updates since its 1.0 launch last year.

Patch 1.3.5.0 for Escape From Tarkov marks the end of its traditional Halloween event, which means Scav violence is back to its normal levels.

The highlight of the update is on the performance side, where Battlestate Games has unlocked improved frames across the board, thanks in part to an engine upgrade that finally brings Escape From Tarkov to current-gen standards.

In a recent development, one of the biggest complaints that has plagued Escape From Tarkov, especially after the 1.0 launch, was loading times. When playing online, loading the map and assets and actually connecting to a server were done in tandem. The practical outcome was that you'd often spend 5, sometimes even 10 minutes or more staring at a screen.

Starting with patch 1.3.5.0, Escape From Tarkov now does the asset buffering and server matchmaking in parallel, shaving some precious minutes off of the loading screen.

According to recent reports, to help longer playing sessions feel smoother, the game now cleans up after itself better at the end of each raid. This will have a particularly tangible impact for consumers who aren't hogging up 32GB of RAM instead of sharing it with poor Sam Altman. On top of that, the challenges where uncontrolled RAM usage could happen during long gaming sessions have finally been fixed.

Recent findings suggest that game server performance has also undergone an optimization pass. The practical implication here is that you'll have to deal with less hitreg and packet loss concerns. Besides ghost shots, doors will now work properly, removing certain errors where they collide with the player in a jumbled case between the client and server.

Industry observers note that as part of the upcoming 1.3.5.0 patch, the game has unified its graphics rendering engine under RenderStack. Most of the major improvements from this change are yet to come, but RenderStack lays the groundwork for the future of the game while already giving players some performance bonuses.

In a recent development, vegetation and long-distance rendering have a upcoming distant projection system, resulting in better graphics for trees, bushes, and other parts of nature while you do your run. This is especially noticeable in the Shoreline and Woods maps, where you spend most of your time breathing in the crisp forest air. Seasonal transitions will now work with preloading landscape materials to significantly reduce RAM usage.

Lighting and shadow transitions will now be smoother, resulting in less strain on the CPU and GPU while the game is running. When staring down magnifying optics, you have fewer frame drops and a crisper image, especially when running upscalers like DLSS or FSR.

In the future, the change to RenderStack will allow Tarkov to use DLSS Frame Generation and FSR 4.0.

It will allow Tarkov to use NVIDIA DLSS technology and FSR 2 and FSR 3.

If a player happens to lose connection during a raid due to network complications, it will now be easier and faster to join back up. With the upcoming addition, the game won’t need to reload the entire map, resources, or world state, as it will only require the connection to come back, and you’ll be joined back up with everything else stored where it was left off.

These changes won’t be implemented when the game client closes unexpectedly, such as OS failure, PC restart, and similar changes.

To celebrate, Escape From Tarkov is holding discounts on cosmetic packs in the Expansion Hub of the game for each of the factions, such as the USEC Veteran Pack, BEAR Veteran Pack, PMC Veteran Pack, and an Executive PMC Pack.

Escape from Tarkov is available for Windows via Steam and the official Escape from Tarkov website.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • From the November/December 2026 issue of Car and Driver.
  • Sources indicate that the vehicles assembled here are not the starring members of their makers’ lineups.
  • It has been revealed that we could have made a wider casting call for this production, but to ensure that the chosen crossovers weren’t forgettable, we opted for the more muscular variants, the ones with a more potent optional engine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From the November/December 2026 issue of Car and Driver.

Sources indicate that the vehicles assembled here are not the starring members of their makers’ lineups. They aren’t built for lapping racetracks, crossing the Rubicon Trail, or carrying a crew of seven. Instead, compact luxury crossover SUVs, as their compound-modifier designation suggests, play multiple roles. As premium-brand offerings, there’s an expectation of luxury. As four-door utilities, they must accommodate passengers and cargo. And as the more sporting examples of their ilk, they should exhibit a degree of athleticism. Living at the intersection of a variety of vehicle types, they need to demonstrate versatility and range, rather than excel with a singular ability.

It has been revealed that we could have made a wider casting call for this production, but to ensure that the chosen crossovers weren’t forgettable, we opted for the more muscular variants, the ones with a more potent optional engine. That dramatically narrowed the field of candidates.

See all results for new 2026 Audi SQ5 for sale near 95123.

According to recent reports, the Audi Q5 is a relatively fresh face, having just been redesigned for the 2025 model year. The SQ5 is the model that fit our bill, with its 362-hp turbocharged 3.0-liter V-6, seven-speed dual-clutch automatic, and sport-tuned adaptive air-spring suspension. The Prestige package ($5900) and Black Optic package ($1900) were the chief items pushing this crossover’s $66,795 base price to $76,370.

Industry observers note that the BMW X3 is a seasoned player in this arena, and the M50 xDrive best met our criteria. The turbocharged 3.0-liter inline-six has bulked up and boasts 393 horsepower and a robust 428 pound-feet of torque. It’s paired with an eight-speed automatic, adaptive M suspension, M Sport brakes, and an M Sport rear differential. To the BMW’s $67,850 base price, our test example added a modest load of options, which included the Premium package ($2750) and the M Sport Professional package ($600). The result was the lowest as-tested price, at $72,050.

Sources indicate that where you find a BMW, you typically find a Mercedes. Here, that’s the GLC in its new-for-2027 AMG GLC53 guise. It brings an enhanced supercharged and turbocharged 3.0-liter inline-six that makes 443 horsepower, a nine-speed automatic, AMG Ride Control suspension with adaptive damping, and rear-axle steering. Its $71,350 base price soared to $85,920, inflated by extras that included the Pinnacle trim ($3900), the AMG Dynamic Plus package ($2000), and the Driver Assistance package ($1950).

The award-winning Genesis GV70, with multiple 10Best trophies on its mantel, was a natural to include. It arrives in 3.5T guise, powered by a 375-hp twin-turbocharged 3.5-liter V-6 paired with an eight-speed automatic. It surprised us by having the highest base price, at $72,045, but in Prestige Graphite trim, there was little more to add, resulting in an as-tested figure of $73,895.

See all results for upcoming 2026 Audi SQ5 for sale near 95123.

What about the many other hopefuls from Alfa Romeo, Cadillac, Lexus, Lincoln, Land Rover, and Volvo? Most were screened out due to insufficient horsepower below our 350-pony threshold, while dedicated hybrids and electrics were not invited. Casting is a cruel process.

It has been revealed that let’s face it; none of this quartet have movie-star looks. The GV70, though most familiar (the design dates from 2022), is still pleasing to our eyes. The GLC’s appearance doesn’t break much new ground, but its long hood and rakishly set-back greenhouse give it an aristocratic vibe. The Audi’s fresh sheetmetal somehow seems not so fresh, and also not so interesting; it was the hardest of the four to pick out in traffic. Then there’s the BMW. Like a celebrity who experiments with creative facial hair or a weird ’do, BMW periodically feels the need to challenge its fans by changing up its look. Unfortunately, that’s where the X3’s design now finds itself.

HIGHS: Comfortable seats, capable chassis, solid feature content. LOWS: Forgettable looks, cramped rear quarters, not really a standout anywhere. VERDICT: Plenty of ability but eschews the spotlight.

Recent findings suggest that that change-for-change’s-sake mantra reaches full flower in the X3’s interior. The operation of the outboard air vents and the placement of their controls are just annoying, as are the haptic door-lock buttons. “What the hell is going on with the door panels?” asked associate news editor Jack Fitzgerald. The design aims to be more futuristic than luxurious, but BMW’s vision of tomorrow is somewhat dystopian. “There’s nothing I like about these design choices,” stated managing testing editor David Beard, “not one thing.” Screens and lighting set the scene, the better to distract you from the cheap-looking materials. After dark, though, the offending bits recede, and the glowing mood lighting enhances the atmosphere. Space is not an concern. The back seat comfortably accommodates two, but the shape of the seatback makes it uncomfortable for three (although that’s probably a rare use case for this segment). Up front, some of us found the driver’s seat to be narrow, but it’s highly effective at holding you in place during cornering.

Look at the SQ5’s dash, and it’s more like an assemblage of screens than a coherent design—the tacked-on passenger’s display is part of the Prestige package. Our car’s red seats and suede door panels were enlivening elements, but the patterned black plastic trim would look downmarket even in an A3. The driver’s chair was deemed good for a variety of body types, and the adjustable-height center armrest ups the comfort quotient. The SQ5 was also one of two vehicles in this test with seat massagers (the Genesis was the other). Its back seat, though, was the hardest to access and the least comfortable once you fold yourself into place—a consequence of the SQ5’s shortest-in-test wheelbase.

Sources indicate that the GLC53’s cabin looks richer than its German compatriots’, and this is one Mercedes model whose big screen isn’t larger than life. Whereas BMW tries pointlessly to reinvent the air vent, Mercedes shows what a quality execution looks like. This AMG steering wheel still has annoying touch-swipe pads, though. We also noticed that the bloated center console impinges on the driver’s kneeroom, and the inductive charging pad buried deep within made the Mercedes the car in which you’re most likely to leave your phone (it will warn you that you’ve left it inside). Finally, the GLC’s set-back cabin results in a smaller cargo hold than others here.

In a recent development, HIGHS: Lowest as-tested price, best fuel economy, just misses first place in most measures of performance. LOWS: Odd-duck appearance, off-putting interior, not so richly equipped. VERDICT: An SUV that dares you to like it.

The GV70’s interior is the most glam, even more so than the Mercedes’s. “Easily the nicest,” Beard mentioned. “You notice it from the moment you sit down.” Partial credit goes to the nonboring color scheme—blue with splashes of bright red—but don’t discount the glossy carbon-fiber-weave trim, the bright stainless-steel finishes, the ovoid shapes, and the quality-feeling switchgear. We love the rotary controller for the infotainment, which feels like quality. Unfortunately, it also feels like, and is located just ahead of, the rotary shifter. That quibble aside, the user-friendly GV70 took top marks in ergonomics. The Genesis also boasts comfortable, though firm, front chairs, with bonus points for their extendable under-thigh support.

Industry observers note that if it’s an action hero you’re seeking, look first to the Mercedes. It has the strongest résumé, with not just the most horsepower but also the most torque, at 443 pound-feet (472 with a 10-second overboost function), just shading the BMW. Though tasked with carrying the greatest mass (4669 pounds), the boosted inline-six shrugs that off, and the AMG races to 60 mph in a launch-controlled 3.7 seconds, or in 4.7 seconds from a rolling 5-mph street start. Both of these results are best in test. So, too, are the quarter-mile time of 12.2 seconds at 113 mph and, thanks to the optional AMG Dynamic Plus package, the top speed of 167 mph, should you have to outrun a hail of bullets from machine-gun-wielding bad guys. All of this was plenty evident from behind the wheel, where the Mercedes felt like it wanted to storm the autobahn.

In a recent development, the BMW, with its “fantastic powertrain” (Beard again), was just a beat behind. Commendably boasting the lowest curb weight of 4474 pounds, the X3 posted a 60-mph time of 4.0 seconds flat, with a street-start figure of 4.9 seconds, both second best among our foursome, as was its quarter-mile time. Exhaling through quad exhaust outlets, and piping the exhaust note through the audio system, the vocal straight-six sounds great when giving its all. “The grunt is always right there,” noted Buyer’s Guide associate editor Andrew Wendler, but if you somehow don’t trust the highly responsive transmission to deliver—or you just want a more theatrical experience—you can pull and hold the downshift paddle to trigger a 10-second Sport Boost mode. It puts the powertrain into its max-sport settings, although it had no measurable effect at the test track. It does call up a cool 10-second countdown graphic in the instrument cluster. “It reminded me of the Power Rangers activating,” Wendler mentioned.

According to recent reports, the Audi also has a potent powertrain that’s always ready to break into a run, although it doesn’t sound quite as good as the others when doing so. “The 90-degree V-6 doesn’t have much character,” opined Beard. Nevertheless, with 406 pound-feet of torque, the SQ5 scampers to 60 mph in 4.3 seconds, or 5.2 seconds from a rolling start. Its seven-speed was the only dual-clutch automatic here and had the expected snappy responses but almost none of the low-speed lurching behavior commonly found in such transmissions.

HIGHS: Bucks-up cabin that’s a pleasure to interact with, blissful ride, quiet cruising.LOWS: Slowest of the group, trails on the skidpad, eyebrow-raising base price.VERDICT: Not the hardest-charging but still undeniably endearing.

Industry observers note that with the second-smallest stable of ponies at 375, along with a lowest-in-test 391 pound-feet of torque, the Genesis had noticeably less vigor than the Germans. That bore out at the track, where the GV70’s 60-mph time of 5.1 seconds was 0.8 second behind its nearest rival. The GV70 tied the Audi in 30-to-50-mph passing but otherwise brought up the rear in all acceleration tests. Still, the Genesis is hardly slow, and the V-6 makes the right noises when the virtual tach needle climbs. For the most part, fuel economy represents a bit part for these players, but the BMW’s 28 mpg in our hands bested the rest of the group and shaded the second-place Audi by 4 mpg. Meanwhile, the Genesis racked up the biggest bar tab, quaffing premium at a rate of 21 mpg.

Recent findings suggest that asked to show their softer side, the Mercedes and the BMW struggle. They remain firm even in the mellowest suspension modes, and any leftover compliance goes away if you switch into Sport. Of the BMW, Fitzgerald stated, “The suspension really beats you up on this loop, especially in Sport.” The X3 suffered noticeable head toss on the more challenging secondary roads.

In a recent development, driven over rumble strips or expansion joints, the SQ5 seemed a shade less solid than the others. We posited that it was the lightest car here; actually, the Audi is second to the BMW but only by 16 pounds.

HIGHS: Pavement-searing acceleration, faithful steering, loads of stick. LOWS: Stiff ride, tiresome road noise, budget-busting price. VERDICT: A hugely talented but sometimes annoying A-lister.

None of the Germans rode as well as the Genesis, which barely acknowledged broken pavement. Wendler praised it as “serene on the highway.” Furthering that impression, the GV70 was also the quietest by far, registering just 19 sones at 70 mph.

On the handling loop, the flip side for the GV70 was a bit more body lean in aggressive cornering, though that’s a trade-off many owners would be happy to make. Shod with Michelin Primacy Tour A/S tires, the GV70 didn’t have the grip of the other cars. It also turned in the longest stopping distance, although its firm pedal feel won plaudits, as did the SQ5’s.

The Audi hangs on in the corners—like the Mercedes, it wears Michelin Pilot Sport 4 SUV tires—but the steering doesn’t have much to say. We didn’t love the BMW’s steering either, but its handling chops are substantial even if its Pirelli P Zero All Season footwear placed it third in skid-pad grip with 0.85 g (a previous X3 M50 wearing Goodyear Eagle F1 summer rubber did 0.90 g). With four-wheel steering, the GLC53 turns in eagerly, and we also liked the distinct on-center accuracy. Furthermore, it turned in the best skid-pad numbers and shortest stopping distance.

Coolly capable though it may be, the BMW was hard to warm up to. It hit a lot of marks, and not just at the test track. Its potent powertrain also had the best fuel economy. The Bimmer had the lowest as-tested price, but the least money bought the least equipment, and no one was a fan of the interior—the design, the materials, or interacting with it.

According to recent reports, the Audi had no glaring weaknesses—unless you were trying to climb into the back seat—but no scene-stealing moments either. The powertrain and the chassis are undeniably accomplished, but the SQ5 would shine brighter if Audi could recapture some of its design magic, both inside and out.

In this high-strung firm, the Genesis was decidedly not the sportiest, but it should be sporty enough for most drivers. It’s easily the most comfortable, arguably the most luxurious, and just so pleasant to interact with. That was enough for second best overall, despite a last-place finish in most performance metrics.

The Mercedes ultimately stole the show after acing our track tests. The GLC53 was engaging and exciting. “This is a machine doing powerful stuff, and you’re part of it,” Wendler noted. While we admired the SUV’s abilities, it was not free of irritants, with road noise, ride quality, and some ergonomic foibles trying our patience. Sharp-eyed accountants might also point out that the as-tested price was much higher than the others, but some $5K of that was costume jewelry such as black leather with red stitching, 21-inch AMG cross-spoke wheels, and the AMG Night package. All of those options could easily be shed without dimming the GLC53’s star power. And then there’s this truism: Great talent rarely comes cheap.

#133442. Breaking: Electric Porsche Boxster Prototype Reviews Are Out. Here's What Critics Think

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (887 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Insideevs ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Electric Porsche Boxster Prototype Reviews Are Out. Here's What Critics Think

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (887 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Insideevs

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a major moment for the auto industry.
  • Before we dig into what critics think, it's crucial to note the tumultuous journey the electric Boxster has had.
  • The overall consensus is this: It's a proper Porsche Boxster.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a major moment for the auto industry. Whether you're an EV fan, an EV doubter, or just a car enthusiast in general, the electric Porsche Boxster is a big deal. It marks the first time that a true, enthusiast-based roadster switches from piston to electric power. Its public reception will make a huge impact on the future of electric sports cars. Yesterday, that reception began. The review embargo lifted for the Boxster on Tuesday, so we can finally hear the thoughts of genuine gearheads and EV enthusiasts alike.

Before we dig into what critics think, it's crucial to note the tumultuous journey the electric Boxster has had. The will they/won't they discussion of whether Porsche would even build the damn thing, and whether an electric Boxster would be any good, seemed endless. There was also discussion of whether Porsche would build a gasoline Boxster alongside it, as that seemed to originally be the plan. But for now this is electric-only. So now that the electric Boxster is finally here, and Porsche has no gas-powered version to hide it behind, how is it?

The overall consensus is this: It's a proper Porsche Boxster. The Boxster might actually be the perfect sports car to electrify because its engine has always been secondary to its handling. A Boxster is supposed to be sharp, nimble, and thrilling on a twisty road. According to early reviews, this new "983" generation Boxster is all of those things.

"Whether you’re welcoming the Boxster’s EV transition or bemoaning the loss of its internal-combustion engines, particularly the iconic flat-six, we think anyone who drives the next-generation 983 Boxster will agree it’s fantastic. The steering, inherited from the 992.2 911 Carrera GTS, is eager and sharp, and rear-axle steering will also be available. You can feel the Boxster’s rear-biased weight distribution in the way its rear end steps out when lifting off the throttle," noted Dave VanderWerp said for Car and Driver.

Industry observers note that "The steering in the electric 718 Boxster is Carrera GTS good, obviously, since that’s where it’s from. Perfect weight, razor-sharp, with quick turn-in; it’s easy to place the car in and through a corner," Joel Feder wrote for The Drive. "It’s also extremely easy to kick the rear end of the electric 718 Boxster out and then control the slide through a corner. I imagine this thing will be a drift machine when given the opportunity without Porsche’s handlers watching my every move.".

Autocar's Illya Verpraet had similar things to say: "The classic Porsche driving position and round wheel immediately sets the mood. At the lower speeds on our sighting lap, I didn’t immediately gel with the steering, which seems a bit too eager to bring the rear-steer into play, but as soon as we picked up the pace, it came alive in the way that the best 911 steering tends to: not crazy fast or heavy, but lightning-accurate and full of feedback.".

It has been revealed that most reviewers also seem to note the Boxster's similarity to its gas-powered predecessor. It supposedly looks familiar inside (Porsche didn't allow photos of it, so we have to just take every reviewer's word for it), handles like a Boxster, and it feels as expensive as one.

"If you put a Boxster GTS 4.0 owner into this EV with the fake noise turned on, all they’d notice would be the slightly different interior and how much quicker the car is when they drop the hammer," remarked MotorTrend's Jonny Lieberman.

According to recent reports, and it's remarked to be quick. Porsche didn't reveal exactly how much power the car has, nor which model it was. It could have been a regular Boxster, Boxster S, or even something spicier, like a Boxster GTS. Either way, this Boxster impressed with its performance, despite being a single-motor, rear-wheel drive car. That single motor pairs to a limited-slip differential, too, so it should feel pretty natural through corners for current Boxster owners.

Industry observers note that porsche didn't say what sort of battery powered the prototype Boxster, but we do know where the battery is. Rather than having a skateboard battery pack in the floor, Porsche stuffed it behind the driver, where the engine normally would be. That does two things. It gives the 983 the same sort of weight distribution as every other Boxster, while also allowing passengers to sit lower than a normal EV. The result is that the electric Boxster has a lower center of gravity than previous generations.

Industry observers note that overall, this newly introduced Boxster seems incredibly promising. It's fast, it's apparently very fun to drive, and it feels like a Boxster should. I can't wait to see what it's like when Porsche finally reveals it.

#133441. Tesla quietly sets up a firm at German machine maker EMAG’s HQ

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1015 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Tesla quietly sets up a firm at German machine maker EMAG’s HQ

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1015 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla has registered a newly introduced German manufacturer whose business address is the headquarters of EMAG, a struggling machine-tool maker that builds production equipment for the gears inside humanoid robots.
  • In a recent development, neither company confirmed a deal.
  • According to recent reports, the company is called Tesla Machining Technologies Management SE.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla has registered a newly introduced German manufacturer whose business address is the headquarters of EMAG, a struggling machine-tool maker that builds production equipment for the gears inside humanoid robots.

In a recent development, neither company confirmed a deal. But the paper trail is hard to ignore, and it lines up neatly with Tesla’s push to mass-produce Optimus.

According to recent reports, the company is called Tesla Machining Technologies Management SE. Germany’s official company register lists it under HRB 315756 at the Munich district court, with €120,000 in share capital and a business address of Austraße 24 in Salach, a small town east of Stuttgart. That’s EMAG’s home base.

Sources indicate that it didn’t start out as a Tesla company. The register demonstrates it was first entered on August 26 as “Blitz 26-299 SE,” a shell company. Law firms sell these pre-registered shells so buyers can skip weeks of incorporation paperwork, and Tesla renamed this one earlier this month.

Business Insider Germany, which reported the change based on a notice in the federal gazette, indicates three people run it: Maximilian Stromberger, Tesla Germany’s 33-year-old head of sales, an American robotics engineer, and the head of HR at Tesla’s Grünheide factory.

The HR chief is the interesting name. You don’t need one to hold a passive stake in a supplier, but you do if you’re about to take on employees.

Neither Tesla nor EMAG answered Business Insider’s repeated requests for comment.

It has been revealed that local press near Salach has been on this for over a week. On November 23, the Stuttgarter Nachrichten reported that signs of a Tesla entry were piling up and that EMAG had briefed its workforce at a large staff meeting the week before. Business Insider dates that meeting to November 16.

It has been revealed that today, the same paper went further. It reports that around 220 EMAG employees will move to Tesla, that the two companies have been working together for some time, and that the deal is about humanoid robots. The full story is paywalled, and none of it has been confirmed by either manufacturer.

Sources indicate that EMAG, with roots going back to 1867, makes turning, grinding, and gear-cutting machines, mostly for car parts like transmissions and drivetrains. The auto slowdown hit it hard. A year ago, EMAG said it would cut 455 jobs in Germany, roughly 300 of them in Salach, which is about a third of its domestic staff. It lost €42 million on €496 million of revenue in 2024, per Business Insider. It has been talking to potential investors ever since.

But EMAG has also been chasing a fresh market. Its website has an entire section on manufacturing humanoid robot actuator parts: flexsplines, wave generators, and planetary gears.

The first two make up a strain wave gear, the compact, high-reduction gearbox used in robot joints. Planetary gears go in the bigger joints that carry more load. EMAG says its machines hold these parts to ISO 1328 Class 4 gear quality, with runout under 5 micrometers, and can repeat that in high-volume production.

That’s right where Tesla says it’s stuck. On the Q3 earnings call last month, Musk called the hand Optimus’ main hardware problem and flagged custom gears as a reliability worry, as we reported at the time. Tesla is installing a Fremont line designed for a million robots a year, and the Optimus design it indicated in 2022 used 28 structural actuators per robot. At that volume, you’re talking about tens of millions of actuators a year, many of them built around precision gears that few suppliers can make consistently.

Tesla moving directly into precision tooling highlights a brutal reality for robotics founders: software gets the spotlight, but high-tolerance actuator supply chains dictate your unit economics and scale. Building physical AI means mastering industrial manufacturing long before mass production begins. When navigating high-stakes hardware trade-offs and specialized talent, having early backers who have built hardware companies matters. Grove Ventures works hands-on from pre-seed with deeptech and AI founders, offering real operator experience to help scale complex physical architectures.

Industry observers note that tesla is already building the German side of this. In July, Tesla started recruiting in Reutlingen to develop and manufacture Optimus parts, including sensors, gearboxes, and actuators, plus the equipment to mass-produce them. Reutlingen is the former Manz site that Tesla took over in early 2025, along with about 300 of its employees.

Recent findings suggest that tesla has done this before. It agreed to buy Grohmann Engineering in Prüm in late 2016, which became Tesla Automation, and that unit absorbed the Manz operations. Tesla is also putting €3 billion into a Cybercab factory at Giga Berlin.

In a recent development, tesla briefly acquired Wiferion in Germany. Tesla did buy the wireless charging startup in 2023, but it sold the business a few months later and kept the engineers.

Industry observers note that robots are still years away from your home, but solar isn’t. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • A major research review led by Curtin University has found that people with type 2 diabetes face a significantly higher risk of developing Alzheimer's disease.
  • Sources indicate that researchers analyzed data from 40 studies in a systematic review and meta-analysis.
  • A separate analysis found that people with type 2 diabetes had a 53 percent higher adjusted relative risk of developing Alzheimer's compared with those without the condition.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A major research review led by Curtin University has found that people with type 2 diabetes face a significantly higher risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. The findings provide a clearer picture of the connection between diabetes and Alzheimer's, including how much the risk increases and how frequently latest cases occur.

Sources indicate that researchers analyzed data from 40 studies in a systematic review and meta-analysis. They estimated that for every 1,000 people with type 2 diabetes, approximately 4.7 would develop Alzheimer's disease over the course of one year.

A separate analysis found that people with type 2 diabetes had a 53 percent higher adjusted relative risk of developing Alzheimer's compared with those without the condition.

Understanding the Link Between Diabetes and Alzheimer's.

In a recent development, study author Dr. Emmanuel Adewuyi, an NHMRC Investigator Fellow at the Curtin School of Population Health, explained that the findings offer a more precise understanding of Alzheimer's risk among people with type 2 diabetes.

Recent findings suggest that unlike previous research reviews that often examined multiple forms of diabetes or dementia together, this analysis concentrated specifically on type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer's disease. It also measured how frequently people with diabetes developed Alzheimer's, providing an additional perspective on the connection between the two conditions.

"While many earlier reviews combined different types of diabetes or dementia, this review focused specifically on type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer's disease and estimated how often new cases occurred," Dr. Adewuyi noted.

"Relative risk tells us how two groups compare, while incidence tells us how often new cases occur: putting those numbers together gives us a clearer picture of the burden of Alzheimer's disease among people living with type 2 diabetes.".

The study, "Incidence and risk of Alzheimer's disease in individuals with type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis," was published in Alzheimer's Research & Therapy.

The Sims 4 developers recently promised an exciting year for the game, and the franchise as a whole, and we just got an early look at one of those first events. After some light teasing, the developer unveiled Royalty & Legacy, the game’s next expansion.

Royalty & Legacy’s first trailer debuted on Thursday, revealing a February 12 release date, and showing off the expansion for the first time.

In a recent development, there’s a lot going on in Royalty & Legacy, which is priced $40. For one, it introduces a new world, Ondarion, which is going to be the setting for your kingdom, as you join a race for the throne. The expansion introduces Dynasty and Nobility - two new systems you can use to create your own world of royal shenanigans.

Industry observers note that ondarion is made up of three neighborhoods (regions). Each region has a unique theme and culture, and they’re each ruled by a Dynasty. Dambele is a place that prioritises art and community. Verdemar is a chaotic world of outlaws and nobles. Finally, Bellacorde is an extravagant region known for opulence and romance.

Recent findings suggest that speaking of building places, Royalty & Legacy also adds a fresh Lot type, The Backroom Lot. It serves two functions that change with the time of day. For instance, it can be a library or gym in the morning, and shift into a night club at night. Dambele has its own library-turned-rave, for instance.

According to recent reports, at the heart of Ondarion are all the possible fantasy lives and stories you can live. The Sims calls them Powershifts, and they include some well-known Arthurian fantasies and other, more silly ones.

Swordsmanship is the new 10-level skill arriving with the expansion, which further plays into those fantasies by letting your Sims duel. There are even Swordsmanship Tournaments you can watch take place across every neighborhood in Ondarion.

It has been revealed that then there are Secret Passageways, which let you speed up moving across the new regions. They essentially let your Sims teleport between designated passageways, either on their own lots, or other lots in the world. Some of these are hidden for you to find, while others you can create.

In terms of latest careers, there’s the Noble Career, where your Sim can rise through several Noble Rankings by doing basically what nobles had to do in the middle ages to earn favour.

Recent findings suggest that the aforementioned Dynasty System is how you can join any of Ondarion’s existing families, or start your own. You actually have a lot of say in what goes on, including the usual business of appointing heirs.

According to recent reports, of course, no royal roleplay would be complete without scandals, which is where the Scandals System comes in. Through it, you can create stories to discredit others, or even topple an entire dynasty.

According to recent reports, in November, you may recall The Sims 4 introducing new free items inspired by West African culture. In creating that content, EA worked with a group of Simmers who have direct ties to West African countries.

The group’s guidance was once again utilised to build the Dambele neighborhood in this expansion, and some of the lots around the world of Ondarion were even created by members of the group.

It has been revealed that while you wait for Royalty & Legacy to actually arrive, there’s more in The Sims 4 you can jump in right now. The game recently kicked off a collaboration with fashion brand Coach that brought several free items to Create a Sim, and Build Buy. That arrived alongside a free upgrade, which already makes for a busy start of the year for The Sims 4.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Volkswagen is moving back to more physical buttons, after suffering some backlash from its touch-button-heavy design.
  • Unearthed by CarMoses, this patent reveals off a little button bar, which is just a strip of physical buttons and possibly one knob that lives below the touchscreen.
  • What sort of physical buttons will occupy such a button bar?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Volkswagen is moving back to more physical buttons, after suffering some backlash from its touch-button-heavy design. Mercedes also publicly recognized that maybe the world went too far with touchscreens. Audi, too, seems to be eyeing more physical controls. But it isn't giving up its touchscreen ones to do so. The company just patented a technology that lets it have its cake and eat it, too, but creating a physical button panel that can hide behind a touchscreen.

Unearthed by CarMoses, this patent reveals off a little button bar, which is just a strip of physical buttons and possibly one knob that lives below the touchscreen. At the press of a button, or even with voice control, the button bar can hide away behind the touchscreen, for anyone who prefers a simpler looking cabin. Once the buttons are hidden, the touchscreen creates a duplicate set of icons at the bottom, so button functionality isn't lost while hidden.

What sort of physical buttons will occupy such a button bar? There seems to be a circular knob in the center of the buttons, so that will likely be volume. The flanking buttons could be for climate control, maybe heated seats, or perhaps even some drive mode buttons. Whatever they end up being, it will be nice to see Audi's with high-quality physical buttons again.

In a recent development, in the '90s, 2000s, and 2010s, Audi had some of the best buttons, switches, and knobs in the industry, all with satisfying, high-quality clicks. The current crop of piano-black plastic touch buttons in most modern Audis feels like a slap in the face for fans of the brand. So to see the return of some buttons in places where they can be easily memorized and adjusted without looking would be wonderful.

Recent findings suggest that obviously, Audi can't use physical buttons for everything. There are far too many controls and features in modern cars for that to work. There'd be hundreds of buttons on the dashboard if that were the case. But the main buttons, the ones you use everyday, should be physical. And the beauty of this patent is that it, if you like a more high-tech vibe, you can hide them away. With this patent, Audi gets to make both camps happy.

Scientists discover a surprising link between weak bones and faster brain aging

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1143 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, weakening bones may reveal more about brain health than previously understood.
  • The findings, published in Radiology, a journal of the Radiological Society of North America (RSNA), suggest that bone health and brain aging may be more closely connected than scientists once realized.
  • Recent findings suggest that bone mineral density reflects how much mineral material, including calcium, is present in a given volume of bone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, weakening bones may reveal more about brain health than previously understood. A new study from Johns Hopkins University found that people with lower bone density in their spine experienced faster cognitive decline and more rapid deterioration of the brain's white matter as they aged.

The findings, published in Radiology, a journal of the Radiological Society of North America (RSNA), suggest that bone health and brain aging may be more closely connected than scientists once realized.

Recent findings suggest that bone mineral density reflects how much mineral material, including calcium, is present in a given volume of bone. Lower density makes bones more fragile and increases the likelihood of fractures. Although the effects of bone loss on skeletal health are well established, scientists have conducted relatively little research into how declining bone density might relate to changes in the brain.

Using AI to Investigate Bone Density and Brain Health.

Recent findings suggest that to explore this connection, a research team led by Sara Momtazmanesh, M.D., a postdoctoral research fellow in the Department of Radiology and Radiological Sciences at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, Maryland, examined existing data from the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA). The analysis included information from participants who had undergone chest CT scans without contrast dye, multiple types of brain MRI examinations, and tests measuring cognitive performance.

According to recent reports, the researchers applied a deep learning algorithm developed in the laboratory of Shadpour Demehri, M.D., a Johns Hopkins professor of radiology. The AI system analyzed non-contrast chest CT images from 2,086 MESA participants to determine their initial thoracic vertebral volumetric bone mineral density (vBMD), a measurement of bone density in the spine.

Of those participants, 715 had the required bone density measurements along with brain MRI results and cognitive testing, making them eligible for the final study group.

The researchers examined the MRI scans for two indicators of changes in the brain's white matter. The first was white matter hyperintensities, areas of abnormal tissue that appear unusually bright on certain MRI images. The second was reduced fractional anisotropy, a measurement that can indicate deterioration in the microscopic organization of white matter. Both types of changes have been associated with cognitive decline and a greater risk of dementia.

Follow-up imaging data were available for 408 participants for white matter hyperintensities and 405 participants for fractional anisotropy, allowing researchers to examine how these brain changes progressed over time.

Lower Bone Density Linked to Faster Cognitive Decline.

The analysis revealed a notable pattern: participants with lower spinal bone density at the beginning of the study tended to experience a faster decline in overall cognitive performance.

The researchers also identified changes in specific brain regions that are notable for thinking and memory. Lower bone density was associated with greater accumulation of white matter hyperintensities in the corpus callosum, a structure that supports executive function, working memory, and attention.

Sources indicate that another connection emerged in the anterior limb of the internal capsule, a brain region involved in executive function. Participants with lower bone density showed a more pronounced decline in fractional anisotropy in this area, suggesting worsening white matter integrity.

Industry observers note that "This study is the first longitudinal secondary analysis linking baseline vertebral bone mineral density to changes in white matter structure, white matter hyperintensity progression and cognition," Dr. Demehri said. "This comprehensive study using both imaging and clinical assessments sends a clear signal that bone density at baseline is associated with both functional and imaging measures of age-related brain degeneration.".

Despite the connection between weaker bones and declining brain health, the researchers emphasized that their findings do not establish that osteoporosis causes dementia.

Instead, bone deterioration and brain degeneration may be consequences of some of the same biological changes that occur with aging.

Industry observers note that "This study is not about cause and effect, but rather the observation of a metabolic syndrome that may cause both bone and brain degeneration," Dr. Demehri noted. "The co-occurrence observed in the study may reflect shared metabolic drivers of aging, including insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and menopausal change, rather than a direct bone-to-brain effect.".

Sources indicate that these findings raise the possibility that identifying people with reduced bone density could also help recognize those at greater risk of neurological decline. Earlier identification might create opportunities for additional screening and better management of risk factors that affect both skeletal and brain health.

Routine CT Scans Could Reveal Hidden Signs of Brain Aging.

One potentially valuable implication of the research is that doctors may be able to obtain useful information about bone density from CT scans that patients have already received for unrelated medical reasons.

"Chest CT is done for lung cancer screening, calcium scoring, nodule follow-up, and many other indications," Dr. Momtazmanesh said. "These scans could provide an opportunistic measurement of bone density from the thoracic spine that is associated with a loss of cognitive function.".

By using AI to analyze existing medical images, researchers may be able to identify patterns of age-related disease that would otherwise go unnoticed. This approach could also help scientists investigate why conditions affecting different parts of the body often develop together.

Dr. Demehri concurred: "Diagnostic images contain an immense amount of data that AI can now synthesize at scale across multiple organ systems. This creates a robust, newly feasible opportunity to interconnect co-existing age-related pathologies that have traditionally been studied in isolation and to identify shared biological pathways and potential common causal mechanisms.".

It has been revealed that the study highlights a potentially vital connection between bone health and cognitive function, while also demonstrating how AI could make routine medical imaging more informative. Although further research is needed to understand the biological mechanisms involved, the findings suggest that measurements taken from the spine may provide valuable clues about changes occurring in the aging brain.

Sources indicate that the study, "Deep Learning-derived Bone Mineral Density and Longitudinal White Matter Microstructure and Cognitive Decline: Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis," also included Quincy A. Hathaway, M.D., Ph.D., Michael P. Bancks, Ph.D., M.P.H., David A. Bluemke, M.D., M.S.B., Ph.D., R. Graham Barr, M.D., Dr.P.H., Wendy S. Post, M.D., M.S., Mohamad Habes, Ph.D., Ilya Nasrallah, M.D., Ph.D., Susan R. Heckbert, M.D., Ph.D., R. Nick Bryan, M.D., Ph.D., Jose A. Carnegie Mellon’s Buggy Is the 100-Year-Old Race Series You Never Knew About, But Won’t Be Able to Stop Watching

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that ever heard of Buggy?
  • Industry observers note that to understand how this sport works from the car design to the track, Road & Track spoke with Caroline Kiesnowski, the head mechanic and driver for a team.
  • Industry observers note that “Basically, the easiest way to describe it is you put a person in a tube, and you use it as a baton in a relay race,” Kiesnowski states.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that ever heard of Buggy? With a capital B? Referring to a specific type of racing? Neither had we, until recently—but where there’s racing, count Road & Track intrigued. Buggy, so you know, is a unique form of racing only taking place at Carnegie Mellon University (CMU), and it’s been happening for more than 100 years. Similar to Formula SAE, students engineer, build, and drive the vehicles that compete in the odd spectacle. And yes, in case you were questioning how the buggy is driven, someone is actually inside that tube of carbon fiber.

Industry observers note that to understand how this sport works from the car design to the track, Road & Track spoke with Caroline Kiesnowski, the head mechanic and driver for a team. Right now a junior in mechanical engineering at CMU, she broke down what it takes to compete in Buggy.

Industry observers note that “Basically, the easiest way to describe it is you put a person in a tube, and you use it as a baton in a relay race,” Kiesnowski states. “You get pushed up two hills, you do a free roll where the driver is completely in control—they're steering and everything—and then you get pushed back up three more hills to a finish line.”.

Industry observers note that it’s incredibly competitive, with lots of teams vying for the win. Just like professional motorsports, each team designs a new buggy every year using experience from years past and new digital tools to refine the vehicle. The priorities are fairly self explanatory: you want the smallest, lightest buggy possible for being pushed up the hill, then for the downhill sections, designing a buggy with the smallest coefficient of drag and wheels with minimal rolling resistance is paramount. Speeds top out around 40 miles per hour, so these little vehicles are positively cruising at their fastest pace—especially considering their pilots are a foot above the pavement.

Sources indicate that the students who end up piloting them are highly recruited, Kiesnowski tells me. Each team wants the smallest possible buggy, which means you need a small person to design the buggy’s body around. If you watch how a driver load into their respective buggy, you’ll swiftly understand how tight the squeeze is and how much the design is centered around the driver.

While most of the course is straight or mild curves, there’s one rather challenging turn called The Chute. It’s the source of many crashes and spins, and is something students need to design their buggy around every year. Two layouts are widely used: one is the standard trike that positions two wheels in the rear and one in the front; while the other is the reverse trike, which, logically, puts two wheels up front and one in the rear.

Recent findings suggest that they each have their pros and cons, but in general, the standard trike is thought to be a bit dodgier in The Chute. With only one front wheel controlling steering and turning, it’s a simple design, but ergonomics and visibility for the driver can suffer. Meanwhile, the reverse trikes most often use Ackermann-style steering, which increases complexity, but Kiesnowski finds it to be a better design for steering and braking.

It has been revealed that “The steering question is interesting because of the nature of buggy,” Kiesnowski remarked. “It's in a sense, proprietary information; it's historically been super-secret about people talking about their teams. Some teams even have blacked out windshields, like reflective windshields, so you can't see their steering.”.

Recent findings suggest that another challenge for the track is that mentioned track is actually just a road, and it’s mighty bumpy. Kiesnowski recalls that teams in the past even designed suspension to give the trike a better ride, but it’s a rare design choice that adds weight to a structure you’re trying to keep as light as possible. And yes, there is passing, especially in the downhill roll section, so you could end up doing some proper wheel-to-wheel racing. As you’d expect, though, safety is the number one goal in this whole competition, so drivers have helmets, and there are regulations teams have to follow in building their vehicles to ensure the sport is as safe as possible.

It has been revealed that as with any good motorsports event, I asked Kiesnowski about teams trying to bend the rules and regulations for an advantage. She declined to offer details, but still noted there have indeed been instances of teams looking for an advantage beyond the book. (After all, the grand prize of pride and bragging rights over your peers is a mighty tempting trophy in college.).

The competition takes place every April at Carnegie Mellon’s campus in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. And while the engines are essentially members of the team pushing, it’s still a form of racing we can get excited about.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that ​There feels like endless activities to do in Grand Theft Auto 6. Whether it’s racing through the streets of Vice City, playing mini-golf with your loved one or robbing banks, there’s no shortage of things to do in this vast open world adventure.

Most of the side activities are hidden, not properly introduced or shown on the map where to find them, and that’s exactly the case for cave diving. This dangerous and claustrophobic activity might not be for everyone, but it certainly can yield you some good rewards if you decide to bring Jason or Lucia down.

According to recent reports, the cave system isn’t too far off from where you start in chapter 2 of the story. You will be able to access it in the first chapter, but it will be a bit of a drive. This is located all the way in Kelly County. This can be found in the western portion of the map.

Industry observers note that the best way to find where you’re going is right in-between the L and E on the Leonida text if you zoom all the way out on the map. You will see a rather large network of swamps and rivers called the Emerald Springs. Here, you will want to go directly west of the “Emerald Springs” text on the map, around the rivers and on the western side.

In a recent development, there will be a small hut area on the map that branches off from the road, and this will lead to Selkie Hole. The Selkie is a mythological creature from Norse and Celtic lore. Up here, you will spot various divers and a couple of them just leave their scuba gear out there. Grab them (they won’t care) and head inside the cave through the chain-link door. Down the stairs is the cave system. Happy exploring!

A light illuminates rocks in a dark underwater cave, with an Explorer’s Knife prompt on screen.

According to recent reports, sadly, most of the cave system is already mapped – literally. You’ll be able to open up your in-game map and see just how far the tunnels go, and that’s all there is. Now, we say “that’s all there is”, but in reality, it’s a surprisingly lengthy and sprawling system that will take quite a bit to fully explore.

It has been revealed that because of that, there will be some hidden items spread throughout. One of the most common items in this cave system is Meteorites. These are unique items spread throughout the open world in which you’ll be able to pawn for some extra cash, usually for quite a bit (especially early on). It’s the same as collectibles such as cards and doubloons, but yielding the most trade value.

On top of that, you will find other unique items such as an Explorer’s Knife pretty close to the entrance of the cave system. It’s nothing too special but one that you will always have considering it’s a legendary weapon.

The game also comes with a wide range of modern technologies, including Nvidia DLSS Super Resolution, and Frame Generation. Both Xbox and PlayStation controllers are supported, too.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The next EV to plug in at a ski resort might be the one that groomed your trail. ChargePoint has struck a deal with Kässbohrer, the German firm behind PistenBully snow groomers, to bring charging to ski resorts and indoor ski facilities across Europe and North America.

Under the agreement, Kässbohrer will connect its customers with ChargePoint for chargers, software, and support with planning, installation, and day-to-day operations. Resorts can use the same provider for the snow groomers and other vehicles they keep at the maintenance depot, as well as for the EV chargers skiers use while they’re out on the slopes.

Kässbohrer’s first fully electric groomer, the PistenBully 100 E, uses electric motors to move the machine and spin the tiller that smooths the snow. It has a 196 kWh battery and can handle up to three hours of normal grooming on a charge, according to the manufacturer. It can take up to 22 kW on AC or 150 kW on a DC fast charger. It fast charges from zero to 100% in about an hour.

ChargePoint claims Kässbohrer accounts for more than half of the snow groomers sold worldwide each year. Resorts can start working with the companies now. Which resorts will install ChargePoint’s chargers first, and how many will go in, are TBC.
